Let
\[
\Omega(x,y)=x_1y_3+x_2y_4-x_3y_1-x_4y_2\in R.
\]
Then \(\omega(x,y)=[t^{m-1}]\Omega(x,y)\).

First observe that an \(N\)-stable \(\mathbb F_q\)-subspace is the same thing as an \(R\)-submodule of \(R^4\). The condition that \(N|_L\) has exactly two Jordan blocks of size \(m\), together with \(\dim_{\mathbb F_q}L=2m\), says exactly that
\[
L\cong R^2
\]
as an \(R\)-module.

Now suppose \(\omega\) vanishes on \(L\times L\). Since \(L\) is an \(R\)-submodule, for any \(x,y\in L\) and any \(a\in R\),
\[
0=\omega(ax,y)=[t^{m-1}]\bigl(a\Omega(x,y)\bigr).
\]
If \(\Omega(x,y)\neq 0\), choose its lowest nonzero coefficient, say at \(t^j\), and take \(a=t^{m-1-j}\). Then the coefficient of \(t^{m-1}\) in \(a\Omega(x,y)\) is nonzero, contradiction. Hence
\[
\Omega(x,y)=0\qquad\forall x,y\in L.
\]
So admissible \(L\)’s are precisely free rank \(2\) totally isotropic \(R\)-submodules of \(R^4\), i.e. Lagrangian \(R\)-submodules.

Reduce modulo \(t\). Any such \(L\) gives a totally isotropic \(2\)-plane
\[
\overline L\subset \mathbb F_q^4.
\]
Conversely, fix one Lagrangian plane \(\overline L\). By an \(\mathbb F_q\)-linear symplectic change of basis, it suffices to count lifts of
\[
\overline E=\langle e_1,e_2\rangle.
\]
Any lift \(L\) of \(\overline E\) projects isomorphically onto
\[
E=Re_1\oplus Re_2,
\]
so it is the graph of an \(R\)-linear map
\[
A:E\to F,\qquad F=Re_3\oplus Re_4,
\]
with \(A\equiv 0\pmod t\). Write \(A\) as a \(2\times2\) matrix. The graph is isotropic iff
\[
u^TAv-(Au)^Tv=0\qquad\forall u,v\in E,
\]
which is equivalent to
\[
A=A^T.
\]
Thus \(A\) is a symmetric \(2\times2\) matrix whose three independent entries lie in \(tR\). Since
\[
|tR|=q^{m-1},
\]
each Lagrangian plane over \(\mathbb F_q\) has
\[
(q^{m-1})^3=q^{3m-3}
\]
lifts.

It remains to count Lagrangian \(2\)-planes in \(\mathbb F_q^4\). In a symplectic vector space, every line is isotropic. For each line \(\ell\), the Lagrangian planes containing \(\ell\) correspond to lines in the \(2\)-dimensional space \(\ell^\perp/\ell\), hence there are \(q+1\) of them. Counting pairs \((\ell,P)\), where \(\ell\subset P\), gives
\[
\#\{\text{Lagrangian }P\}
=
\frac{\#\{\text{lines in }\mathbb F_q^4\}(q+1)}{q+1}
=
\frac{q^4-1}{q-1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\#\{\text{Lagrangian }P\}
=
q^3+q^2+q+1
=
(q+1)(q^2+1).
\]

Multiplying by the number of lifts,
\[
\boxed{q^{3m-3}(q+1)(q^2+1)}.
\]
